More illustrations from methods and checklists

These examples were previously embedded in theory, method tables and checklists. The six chapters above are the main story; the illustrations below are optional.

Worked examples6 illustrationsHow the team contributesSee how these methods apply to the asset-management case.Explore the examplesClose the examples

Product, Design, Engineering and AI assistance. Read these only when relevant.

Worked exampleProduct’s investment recommendation

Product reviews the spreadsheet problem and the walkthrough of the asset register. It recommends investing in more accurate records and reliable follow-up. AI can draft alternative ways to achieve that outcome.

Worked exampleDesign’s reporting study

Design watches members report asset changes and Maya review the annual check. It looks at how people:

  • hand an asset to another member;
  • report an asset that is lost or faulty;
  • find and act on reports that need follow-up.

AI can suggest clearer wording for these choices. Design checks that the wording matches what users need to report.

Worked exampleEngineering’s feasibility checks

Engineering uses a test environment to check:

  • who can view or change each project’s records;
  • whether spreadsheet imports preserve the correct assignments;
  • whether a handover takes effect only after acknowledgement;
  • whether retrying the yearly background job preserves existing tasks and responses.

AI can help inspect the code and interfaces and draft test cases.

Worked exampleOptional AI support for fault reports

If the team later adds AI to help draft or sort fault reports, specialists check its suggestions against reports kept separate from development. They check how sensitive details are handled and whether the scoring method is reliable. The core application and annual schedule follow predefined rules.

Worked exampleData access and decision authority

Risk and compliance specialists confirm:

  • which project and member records each role may access;
  • how long the records may be kept;
  • who may authorise inspections and repairs.

AI can link reviewed evidence to the relevant controls. Specialists check those links.

Worked exampleThe agent’s permitted work

An agent can draft a reporting prototype and test the annual workflow in an isolated environment. People still decide whether to fund the pilot and confirm physical inspections. The agent needs separate authorisation to access the live register.

Worked examples2 illustrationsFraming and evidence checksSee how these methods apply to the asset-management case.Explore the examplesClose the examples

Problem statements and research evidence. Read these only when relevant.

Worked exampleIncomplete problem statements
  • An aspiration: “We want complete asset accountability.” This describes a goal without explaining the difficulty. Ask who is struggling to account for equipment and what gets in their way. Record the current result before setting an improvement target.
  • A proposed solution: “We need an asset management app.” This chooses a solution before explaining the need. Ask people to show where the current reporting process fails. Keep the problem statement open to different responses, including changes to the process or existing tools.
  • An end-of-life notice: “The spreadsheet automation will lose support.” Ask the system owner when support ends and what will stop being maintained. Explain how that could affect the service and what could keep it running safely. A confirmed future risk can justify planning a replacement before users experience a failure.
  • A vague complaint: “Our asset spreadsheet is always out of date.” Ask a member to show a recent update that went wrong. Record what happened and how often similar problems occur. Keep that observation separate from explanations that still need checking.
Worked exampleAn unsupported AI summary

AI summarises the brief as “Members lose assets because spreadsheets are unreliable.” The brief says members lack a direct reporting route. It does not say how many assets are lost or why. Compare the claim with the original notes and the register walkthrough before relying on it.

Count a forwarded fault email and its original as one report. If the summary leaves out a member’s difficulty using the form, restore that finding. Design records what the notes support and what remains unclear. Engineering checks any proposed technical cause. Use the remaining question to choose the next observation or test.

Worked examples8 illustrationsChallenging a proposalSee how these methods apply to the asset-management case.Explore the examplesClose the examples

Critique questions and alternatives. Read these only when relevant.

Worked exampleEvidence of reporting difficulties

The brief says members have no direct way to report changes. Walk through the register with them to check how often old assignments or delayed fault reports cause difficulty.

Worked exampleThe cost of keeping the current workflow

Use the current spreadsheet, messages and manually arranged annual check as the starting comparison. Include the time Maya spends chasing replies and the cases still awaiting action.

Worked exampleDifferent users and access needs

Check whose experience differs:

  • members who use equipment in the office;
  • members who work remotely or share equipment;
  • managers who maintain the register;
  • members with different access needs.

Some projects may already have a system that meets their needs.

Worked exampleAlternative reporting solutions

Compare three ways to collect and follow up reports:

  • a form with controlled access;
  • an existing asset platform configured for the project;
  • a dedicated application.

Test the important differences before choosing what to build.

Worked exampleAssumptions behind self-service reporting

Can members identify the right asset? Will Maya have time to act on their reports? Test both assumptions: easier reporting helps only if it produces records people can use.

Worked exampleA small test of the proposed workflow

Test a small declaration flow with “not with me” and “faulty” choices. Separately, interrupt and retry the yearly background job in a test environment. These checks can reveal problems before the team builds the full application.

Worked exampleConflicting goals and growing workloads

A target of “everyone confirms every asset is working” could discourage honest reports. Test what happens when:

  • a member reports an asset that is missing or faulty;
  • many annual tasks and reminders run at once;
  • the number of reports exceeds the manager’s follow-up capacity.
Worked exampleAI-assisted comparison of alternatives

Give AI the brief and the reviewed walkthrough notes, along with project rules it is permitted to use. Ask it to suggest ways members could report changes:

  • a form;
  • an existing asset platform;
  • a dedicated application.

Generated personas can help rehearse research questions, but they provide no observations of actual users.

Compare each suggestion on the same basis:

  • the outcome it could improve;
  • accessibility and permissions;
  • Maya’s workload;
  • build and operating costs;
  • technical limits.

Product records disputed assumptions. Design checks the complete user journey. Engineering reviews the test findings before the team recommends an investment.

Worked examples12 illustrationsApplying experiment methodsSee how these methods apply to the asset-management case.Explore the examplesClose the examples

Twelve ways to learn from small tests. Read these only when relevant.

Worked exampleAn invitation to test asset reporting

Show eligible members a “Try reporting an asset change” link beside the current register guidance. Count how many see it and ask to join the research. When selected, explain that this is a research invitation; it does not submit an actual loss or fault report.

Worked exampleTwo messages for the same audience

Compare “Keep your assigned assets up to date” with “Report changes and complete your annual declaration”. Show the messages to comparable audiences and measure research sign-ups from eligible members and managers. Record how each audience was allocated and where it saw the message.

Worked exampleThree realistic usability tasks

In the first usability test, ask each member to:

  • hand a monitor to another member;
  • report a faulty laptop;
  • answer an annual task for an asset they cannot find.

Record whether each response is accurate and where people need help. Check keyboard access and whether Maya can follow up. Identify any actions the prototype only simulates.

Worked exampleA manually operated reporting service

Tell participants that a coordinator will run the trial service manually. The coordinator:

  • receives reports of handovers, lost assets and faults;
  • updates a trial register with controlled access;
  • prepares the annual list of cases needing Maya’s attention.

Measure record accuracy, follow-up time and the effort needed to run the service.

Worked exampleA simulated annual task queue

A researcher operates the annual task queue behind the prototype. Brief participants and explain the simulation afterwards as agreed in the research plan. Observe whether members understand their response choices. Sending reminders manually does not test whether the scheduler is reliable.

Worked exampleA technical trial with fictional records

Import fictional asset records and check:

  • access within and across projects;
  • handovers accepted at the same time;
  • annual task creation and reminder retries;
  • behaviour around due dates.

Inspect saved records and audit history as well as the response shown on screen.

Worked exampleAn offline evaluation of fault-report assistance

For an optional AI aid that sorts faults and drafts reports, use reports kept separate from development. Include unclear symptoms and descriptions containing misleading instructions. Compare its suggestions with the simple form over repeated trials. Score whether it preserves the member’s facts and whether it attempts unauthorised changes separately.

Worked exampleValue testing in the pilot project

After release checks, pilot reporting in one project during an agreed declaration window. Track:

  • whether recorded holders and asset condition match the evidence;
  • follow-up on lost and faulty assets;
  • overdue replies and unresolved cases;
  • the time Maya spends managing the work.

A rehearsal with an accelerated clock cannot show how well the service works over a full year.

Worked exampleA comparison across project groups

With enough eligible projects, randomly assign projects to the current reporting route or the new application. Ask an experiment specialist to agree the sample and when to stop the test. Shared assets or a manager serving both groups may affect the comparison. Measure record accuracy and follow-up as well as use of the application.

Worked exampleFour layout and wording combinations

Compare two asset layouts, a list and cards, with two versions of the condition question. This gives four combinations. Collect enough observations to compare accurate completion and see whether layout changes the effect of the wording. The first study’s eight members are too few for that estimate.

Worked exampleA limited release with stop conditions

Release the reviewed build to one project first. Watch for:

  • changes made without permission;
  • duplicate annual tasks or missed reminders;
  • faults left overdue;
  • failures when the background job restarts.

If writes need to stop, preserve the live register and the evidence. Monitoring a rollout does not by itself show that the application caused an improvement.

Worked exampleAdaptive reminder timing

In a later experiment, test whether changing the reminder channel or timing helps members respond. Compare it with a fixed schedule using a method suited to changing allocations. Keep contact times and opt-out rules within agreed limits, and preserve accessible routes. Members still provide their own declarations; reminder changes should not fill in answers for them.

Worked examples34 illustrationsTechnical, framework and measurement casesSee how these methods apply to the asset-management case.Explore the examplesClose the examples

Optional deep-dive applications. Read these only when relevant.

Worked exampleA complete task across three solutions

Compare the same complete task in:

  • a managed form;
  • a configured asset platform;
  • a custom application.

Follow an imported assignment through a member’s report to Maya’s follow-up. Separately check the background job that opens annual declarations.

Worked exampleProject access after changes

Use fictional members and managers in two projects to check:

  • access to their own project’s records;
  • denied access to another project’s records;
  • access after an asset changes holder;
  • access after a member leaves.

Keep the allowed and denied results with the audit history. Exclude unrelated member details.

Worked exampleAnnual scheduling and retry checks

Use a controlled clock and simulate job interruptions and notification failures. Check that:

  • each annual run keeps the same identity on retry;
  • each asset has one current task and saved responses survive retries;
  • due dates work as intended;
  • a transfer during the annual check reaches the correct person.

Record software versions and test load, and explain how the environment differs from production.

Worked examplePilot cost ranges

Estimate a range for each cost:

  • cleaning and importing spreadsheet data;
  • configuring an existing platform or building the application;
  • connecting identity and notification services;
  • hosting and supporting the service;
  • following up reports.

Check whether a higher migration estimate would put the pilot over its agreed budget.

Worked exampleAI drafting compared with a simple form

The core application records the holder and condition in structured fields. Compare any optional AI drafting aid with that form. Check:

  • urgent faults it misses;
  • facts it invents or changes;
  • the corrections members need to make;
  • the cost of each useful report after review.
Worked exampleResearch alongside delivery

While Engineering builds the pilot project, Product and Design investigate:

  • how shared equipment is recorded;
  • what happens when members leave;
  • whether Maya can keep up with follow-up.

Add import and scheduling findings to the same research backlog. Record decisions about material changes to scope.

Worked exampleThe job behind an asset report

Ask a member about a recent handover and Maya about chasing annual replies. A possible job statement is: “When an asset changes hands or develops a fault, I need to record the change and know who will follow up.” Ask how much effort reporting takes, how confident people feel and whether fear of blame affects reports of loss.

Worked exampleDouble Diamond for asset reporting

Apply the Double Diamond to the reporting problem:

  • Discover how members use spreadsheets, messages and physical checks;
  • Define the difficulty those observations support;
  • Develop alternatives using a form, an existing platform or an application;
  • Test a small version of the most promising approach.

Revisit the problem if assets cannot be identified reliably or nobody has capacity to follow up.

Worked exampleA five-day reporting sprint

Use the five-day sprint to focus on the member and manager experience:

  • Monday: map the current journey;
  • Tuesday: sketch possible solutions;
  • Wednesday: choose a storyboard;
  • Thursday: build the prototype;
  • Friday: test it with users.

Investigate the annual background job separately; the prototype screens simulate its behaviour.

Worked exampleA small build–measure–learn cycle

Build the smallest flow that lets members report changes and answer an annual task. Check whether members can report accurately and Maya can find their reports. Revise the flow after the first test, then test again. Collect separate evidence for the service’s annual benefit and readiness for live use.

Worked exampleAn opportunity tree for accurate records

Start with the outcome of a current, reliable register. Investigate three opportunities:

  • handovers that never reach the register;
  • fault reports left in messages;
  • annual checks that depend on Maya starting them manually.

Compare the form, platform and application options. Link each option to the interview, usability test or technical check that tests its key assumption.

Worked exampleMissing details in a fault report

A member tells the optional assistant, “My assigned monitor is faulty.” The assistant needs the asset ID and observed symptoms before drafting the report. It asks for missing details and keeps any diagnosis or inspection claim out of the report unless supported.

Worked exampleMember confirmation before submission

Show the draft fault report to the member and ask whether to submit it. If the member declines, save no report. Keep actions on other people’s assets and repair purchases outside the assistant’s agreed permissions.

Worked exampleReport status and repair status

Check that the assistant distinguishes these recorded states:

  • a draft awaiting confirmation;
  • a submitted fault report;
  • follow-up assigned to Maya;
  • a completed repair.

A submission confirmation does not mean the repair is complete.

Worked exampleRecovery after a submission timeout

After a timeout, look up the report using its request ID before retrying. Check for:

  • a duplicate fault report;
  • a change to the wrong asset;
  • an asset transferred to another member;
  • access revoked while the task was running.
Worked exampleMember correction and manager takeover

Let the member read and correct the report. If Maya takes over, give her the original description, current status and history. Preserve a reported problem until someone resolves it; never silently change it to “present and working”.

Worked exampleAn optional fault-report assistant

For a later, optional reporting assistant, test whether it can draft a fault report and submit it after the member confirms. Include:

  • a missing asset ID;
  • unclear symptoms;
  • a member declining submission;
  • an asset transferred to another member;
  • a timeout after the report is accepted.

Check that it asks for missing information and looks up the saved report before retrying. Inspect both the report and Maya’s queue. Record invented details, duplicate reports and the effort needed to take over. This feature remains outside the reviewed PRD. It cannot confirm a physical inspection or submit an annual declaration without the member’s knowledge.

Worked exampleLinks from requirements to tests

An accurate register depends on two requirements: visible member updates and reliable annual declarations. The design gives each asset one current task in each annual check. The retry test checks whether a saved declaration survives another run. The access test checks whether a member can change only the records they are permitted to use.

Link the requirements and design to the reviewed data structures and executable tests. When a handover rule changes, review:

  • the affected screens;
  • handling during an annual check;
  • the related acceptance tests.

Update the information supplied to agents after those records agree.

Worked exampleA decision about a departing member

Maya asks what happens if a member leaves during the annual check. Attach her comment to PRD v0.3 and name the decision owner and response deadline. Record whether the outstanding task returns to Maya, explain the reason and update the affected tests. AI can summarise the discussion; Product checks the original comment and confirms the decision before publishing the revised PRD. Keep the earlier rule in the history and limit access to member details.

Worked exampleSuccessful reporting and follow-up

Can members accurately report who holds an asset and whether it works? Can Maya find the report and resolve the issue without information getting lost between channels?

Worked exampleValue to the organisation

Investigate whether the application helps achieve:

  • a more accurate register;
  • earlier inspection or repair follow-up;
  • less time spent chasing annual replies.

Collect evidence before claiming that it reduces asset loss or saves money.

Worked exampleReporting behaviours to track

Track the work across both the application and previous reporting channels:

  • acknowledged handovers;
  • reports of lost or faulty assets;
  • annual responses;
  • Maya’s follow-up actions.
Worked exampleEarly signals of improvement

Track these early signals:

  • time between an asset change and its report;
  • reminders successfully delivered;
  • annual tasks completed.

Check whether they are associated with more accurate holder and condition records. An increase alone does not establish value.

Worked exampleTime and cost of reaching a decision

Follow the reporting question through both usability tests to the pilot decision. Record:

  • total elapsed time;
  • time contributed by members, Maya and the research team;
  • prototype, engineering and review costs.
Worked exampleFailures reported separately

Report important failures separately:

  • changes to another project’s records;
  • a declaration incorrectly labelled as a physical inspection;
  • missed annual checks or duplicate tasks;
  • faults left without follow-up;
  • accessibility problems;
  • costs above the agreed limit.
Worked exampleResources used by the pilot

Record the resources used for the reporting and annual-check pilot:

  • delivery and research time;
  • spreadsheet cleanup effort;
  • test notifications and hosting costs.
Worked exampleBehaviour linked to accurate records

Check whether more members acknowledge handovers and submit accurate declarations on time. Then check whether those actions lead to current records and completed follow-up.

Worked exampleA measure of reliable asset records

Measure the share of assets in scope whose holder and condition have been checked against evidence and whose reported problems have a recorded resolution. Report completion, overdue work and effort alongside that measure.

Worked exampleEquipment availability and wider outcomes

Check whether the team can account for project equipment and use it when needed. Include the time taken to arrange inspections and repairs. Establish that connection before crediting the application with reducing loss or disruption.

Worked exampleSMART targets and service efficiency

Use SMART to make the pilot target clear:

  • Specific: name the project and reporting window;
  • Measurable: compare results against the versioned asset roster;
  • Achievable: account for Maya’s capacity to follow up;
  • Relevant: measure accurate holder and condition records;
  • Time-bound: agree due dates and a review date.

Collect a baseline before setting numerical improvement targets. More completed declarations are not a success if they hide lost or faulty assets.

For a later fictional cost comparison, use the same scope and cost boundaries:

  • 80 reconciled records per month at S$400 total service cost gives 0.20 records per dollar;
  • 100 records at S$450 gives about 0.222 records per dollar;
  • That is about an 11% improvement in records per dollar.

This measures service efficiency, not financial return on investment. If all records are already reconciled, keep essential reporting and audit functions working before moving investment elsewhere.

Worked exampleTime to a reviewed learning decision

Measure the time from asking whether members can declare accurately to the reviewed decision after the second usability test.

Worked exampleThe full cost of two test cycles

Include the full cost of both test cycles:

  • participation by members and Maya;
  • research and prototype work;
  • technical investigations and computing;
  • review and corrections.
Worked exampleTime spent learning and coordinating

Use the same total team time when comparing effort spent learning with effort spent documenting and coordinating. Count observation and decisions based on evidence consistently, so the comparison is meaningful.

Worked exampleProduct limits alongside outcomes

Monitor these limits alongside the outcome measures:

  • unauthorised changes;
  • missed or duplicate annual tasks;
  • unresolved faults or false inspection records;
  • slow responses and excessive costs;
  • loss of user trust.

Investigate serious individual failures even when the averages improve.

Reference toolkit · Optional

Explore methods when you need them

This library is not a seventh discovery step. Pick the technique that answers your next question. Read the playbook or follow the worked example.

Use these references when a learning question needs more detail. Return to the relevant step with the findings; these references do not add mandatory stages.

Reference: compare twelve experiment methods

Product School’s experimentation playbook [7] covers split tests, multivariate tests, demand probes, landing pages, usability prototypes, manual simulations, staged rollouts and adaptive personalisation. The catalogue below adds technical and operational tests, with recommended evidence limits for each.

Experiment catalogue for business and technical research
MethodQuestion and signalLimits and technical follow-up
Fake-door or smoke testQuestion and signalDoes an early-access offer attract interest? Compare eligible exposures with selections or requests to participate.Limits and technical follow-upExplain availability when users select the offer. Interest does not establish sustained value, willingness to pay or build feasibility. Avoid implying that a consequential action has completed.
Landing page or message testQuestion and signalWhich value proposition attracts the intended audience? Record qualified visits, enquiries and sign-ups.Limits and technical follow-upRecord the audience and acquisition channel. Recruitment bias or different traffic can explain changes; use controlled allocation when claiming one message outperforms another.
Prototype and task-based usability testQuestion and signalCan users complete the intended task? Observe comprehension, errors, completion, assistance and recovery.Limits and technical follow-upA small qualitative study can reveal friction, but cannot estimate improvement across the user population. Note simulated behaviour and untested access needs.
Concierge testQuestion and signalDoes a service help when people deliver it openly? Observe outcomes, repeat use and the effort required to provide support.Limits and technical follow-upRecord manual effort and cost. Treat this as a test of service value; separately establish whether automation can reproduce the useful result.
Wizard of Oz test
Method guidance [12]		Question and signalHow do users interact with an apparently automated interface whose responses are supplied by a person? Observe expectations and task behaviour.Limits and technical follow-upAgree the participant briefing and debriefing in the research plan. Keep operator responses within plausible system limits; a skilled human’s output does not validate a model or integration.
Technical spike or proof of conceptQuestion and signalCan a critical capability or integration work under specified conditions? Run an executable check and measure the relevant limits.Limits and technical follow-upTest the real dependency where permitted. Record mocks, environment differences, test data, versions, failure cases and reproducible results. It does not establish demand.
Offline AI evaluationQuestion and signalCan the model or agent meet the agreed task criteria? Compare the AI with a simpler approach on cases kept separate from development and tuning.Limits and technical follow-upRecord model, prompts, data, retrieval and tool versions. Repeat variable behaviours and inspect failure cases. Offline quality does not establish adoption or production safety.
Proof-of-value pilotQuestion and signalDoes the concept improve a real workflow for a bounded group? Track task outcomes, repeat use and total service cost.Limits and technical follow-upUse a credible baseline or comparator and record selection effects. Include support and correction effort; plan deeper evaluation if the pilot cannot isolate the cause of improvement.
A/B or split test
Design guidance [13]		Question and signalDoes a defined change improve a chosen outcome? Randomly allocate eligible units to control and treatment, then estimate the difference.Limits and technical follow-upConfirm instrumentation, allocation unit, adequate sample and a planned stopping rule. Check guardrails and uncertainty; a small statistically detectable change may still have little practical value.
Multivariate test
Method guidance [14]		Question and signalWhich combination of factors works, and do they interact? Compare planned combinations, such as content and layout variants.Limits and technical follow-upPlan enough observations for the combinations. Use a simpler experiment when traffic is limited; changing several elements without a designed comparison obscures their effects.
Canary or beta rolloutQuestion and signalHow does an implemented change behave under limited exposure? Observe reliability, task outcomes, support demand and recovery.Limits and technical follow-upApply the release checks and stop criteria. Rollout monitoring alone is not a causal comparison. Keep an explicit control design when testing an improvement claim.
Adaptive personalisationQuestion and signalDoes a changing allocation policy improve outcomes across relevant users? Evaluate the policy and important segments over time.Limits and technical follow-upUse a comparison and analysis suited to adaptive allocation, with specialist input. Set exploration limits and guardrails; automatic adaptation alone does not demonstrate benefit.
Reference: test technical assumptions as concepts emerge

Test feasibility alongside user value

Ask Engineering: “What could prevent this solution working, and what small test would tell us?” For Maya’s application, the answer may be whether a handover can change the correct record without exposing another project’s assets. This is SVPG’s feasibility risk [3]: whether the team can build the solution with its available time, skills and technology.

Engineering leads the investigation with Product, Design and the affected service owners. Product agrees which decision the result will inform, the time limit and what remains unknown. Use this checklist when a candidate raises a technical question.

Technical assumptions to resolve before a bounded commitment
AssumptionCheck and retained evidence
The critical path can workCheck and retained evidenceCompare reuse, purchase and build options. Exercise the uncertain interface or capability; retain executable results, versions, dependency owners and untested conditions.
Data and actions are permittedCheck and retained evidenceTest identity, data access and action boundaries with representative permitted and denied cases. Record missing access and decisions needed from accountable owners.
The service can meet operating limitsCheck and retained evidenceMeasure response time (latency), expected workload, failures and recovery. State test conditions, quality targets and differences from the intended environment.
Delivery and operation are affordableCheck and retained evidenceEstimate build, integration, migration, support and exit costs as ranges. Confirm skills, capacity and external lead times; record assumptions and sensitivity.
AI adds useful capability, where proposedCheck and retained evidenceCompare the AI with a simpler approach on representative cases kept separate from development and tuning. Retain model, prompt and data versions, failure cases, human correction effort and cost per successful task.

If an important technical question remains open, run a short investigation, often called a spike. Agree its question, owner, test environment, success criteria and budget. Report what ran, what failed and what remains unknown. A simulated integration can show how an interaction works while leaving the real connection untested. Test the actual dependency separately. Carry the findings into the technical requirements document (TRD) when preparing the technical design.

Reference: use the Double Diamond to widen and narrow choices
Reference: Project Discovery frameworks

Choose a framework for the question

You can use the six steps without choosing a named framework. A framework helps organise the work; a method gathers evidence about a question. Open this reference when you need another way to approach a difficulty. Product School’s Project Discovery guide [6] introduces the approaches below.

The table shows where each approach helps and the working artefact to retain. Use the originating sources for each framework; the JTBD row also links the Christensen Institute’s account [18]. Investigate feasibility and review the evidence whichever framework you use.

Project Discovery frameworks and how to apply them
FrameworkUse and working artefactTechnical investigation connection
How do we keep learning during delivery?
Continuous discovery and delivery
SVPG [10]		Use and working artefactUse when learning continues alongside implementation. The same Product, Design and Engineering contributors investigate upcoming options while delivery develops bounded, supported scope. Keep a shared learning backlog and decision record. Cagan’s article now favours continuous discovery and delivery over its older “Dual-track Agile” label, to emphasise principles rather than process.Technical investigation connectionRoute integration, operating-cost and quality findings back into Project Discovery. Keep collaboration active through handover; separate workstreams do not require separate teams.
Do we understand the progress users seek?
Jobs To Be Done
Christensen Institute [18]		Use and working artefactUse when the underlying need is unclear. Investigate the circumstances, the progress users seek, its functional, social and emotional dimensions, and why current alternatives fall short. Retain an evidence-linked job statement.Technical investigation connectionExplore constraints in the user’s actual setting, including access, devices, connectivity and workarounds. Keep the desired outcome independent of a preferred technology.
Are we choosing a solution too early?
Double Diamond
Design Council [2]		Use and working artefactUse when the team is converging too early. Discover and Define expand and narrow the problem; Develop and Deliver explore and test responses. Retain problem and concept alternatives with reasons for narrowing them.Technical investigation connectionExplore reuse, process changes and different technical approaches before commitment. See the Double Diamond explanation.
Can we test one focused question this week?
Design Sprint
GV [11]		Use and working artefactUse for a focused question with available participants and decision makers. The five-day format maps the challenge, sketches options, chooses a direction, prototypes and tests it. Retain the storyboard, prototype and observations.Technical investigation connectionInvolve Engineering in choosing the testable slice. Run a separate spike for simulated integrations; the sprint’s prototype findings do not settle implementation feasibility.
How do we repeat a useful learning cycle?
Lean Startup
Build–Measure–Learn [9]		Use and working artefactUse repeated learning cycles when the value proposition or operating model is uncertain. Choose an assumption, build the smallest credible test, measure the result and decide whether to persevere or change direction. Retain the hypothesis, measures and decision.Technical investigation connectionInclude build, run and support cost in the learning. A minimum viable product (MVP) used by real users still needs the controls appropriate to its data, actions and exposure.
How do we connect needs, options and tests?
Opportunity Solution Tree
Teresa Torres [8]		Use and working artefactUse to connect a desired outcome to researched user opportunities, alternative solutions and assumption tests. Retain the tree and links to evidence; compare several responses to the selected opportunity.Technical investigation connectionAttach feasibility assumptions and spike results to solution branches. Keep user opportunities distinct from implementation tasks or a list of requested features.

Combine only the practices the decision needs

For a complex question, interviews can clarify the task, an opportunity tree can organise alternative responses, and a focused sprint can test an interaction. Use Build–Measure–Learn to repeat the experiments and continuous discovery to keep learning connected to delivery. Record the question, evidence and next decision rather than treating framework completion as progress.

When agents use the product: test their journey

Test the experience when an agent acts for a user

Worked exampleCheck an agent submitting Alex’s fault report

Suppose an agent drafts a fault report for Alex. Can he check the asset and description before submission? If the request times out, can the agent check whether it succeeded before trying again? Alex needs to see the result and take over when the agent cannot finish.

When an agent operates the product, test the complete task as well as its individual operations. Sumit Sheth calls this agentic user experience (AUX): designing how agents use a product alongside its human experience. Exposing an API alone does not show that the task works.

The following are suggested Project Discovery checks for such products. For software that only uses AI during development, continue with the usual user and service journeys.

Suggested checks for a journey carried out by an agent
Part of the journeyWhat to test
Task and informationCan the agent identify the intended task, obtain permitted context and ask for missing information without inventing it?
Permission and controlCan the user see the proposed action, set its scope, give any required approval and stop further work?
Action and resultCan the agent choose the appropriate operation and distinguish a completed task from a request that was merely accepted?
Failure and recoveryWhat happens after a timeout, partial completion, ambiguous instruction or denied access? Check that a retry does not duplicate a consequential action.
Explanation and human takeoverCan the user inspect what changed, correct the result, recover where possible and take over with enough context?

Record the model, tool interface, permissions and test conditions with the prototype version. Repeat variable behaviours and inspect the resulting system state. Use the AI evaluation guidance to plan deeper checks during implementation.

Advanced: link intent, decisions and requirements
Worked exampleKeep the reason beside the requirement

Members choose the wrong asset status in the test. The team changes the response choices. The requirement keeps each answer distinct; the acceptance check confirms that each answer reaches Maya’s queue correctly. Linking those records helps the next team understand why the behaviour matters.

Product intent explains why a product exists, what it should do and which limits apply. Keep the evidence, requirements, designs, decisions and open questions linked. Review contradictions before using these records as context for an agent.

Link the intended outcomes to product behaviour and the architecture that supports it. Show how policy and evaluation apply across those links:

  • a product behaviour exists because it supports a user and business outcome;
  • an architecture choice exists because it enables required behaviour under known constraints;
  • a policy control exists because it addresses a defined risk; and
  • an evaluation shows whether the intended behaviour and constraints are met.

Name who keeps the product record current and retain earlier versions with their decisions. A reviewer should be able to follow a requirement back to its reason and evidence.

Use automatically checked records where useful

Teams using automated checks can also express relevant requirements in API descriptions, data schemas, policy rules, acceptance tests or evaluation datasets. These machine-readable records help tools check specific conditions; they complement the explanation of the user need.

Record feedback and decisions between meetings

Attach feedback to a specific version of the brief, prototype or PRD. State the question, response deadline and decision owner. Keep one linked decision record with the date, options considered, evidence, rationale, actions and superseded decisions.

Link relevant comments and discussion notes from that record. Check AI-generated summaries against the original notes before relying on them, and confirm material decisions with their owners. Use recordings only where permitted, with agreed access and retention.

A useful specification makes assumptions, constraints, permissions, non-functional requirements, edge cases and exclusions explicit. Increase precision as uncertainty falls, and revise intent when evidence changes. Read about spec-driven development. GitHub Spec Kit’s methodology [4] advocates versioned specifications, linked technical plans and feedback from implementation; treat this as a proposed method and verify generated code against the requirements.

Advanced: connect measures to value

Draw on several kinds of evidence

  • User evidence: interviews, usability studies, support cases and co-creation sessions.
  • Behavioural evidence: product analytics, controlled experiments, workflow completion and adoption.
  • Operational evidence: telemetry, reliability, latency, incidents, model traces and recovery.
  • Evaluation evidence: offline datasets, automated tests, agent evaluations, policy checks and calibrated model-based judges.
  • Cost evidence: experiment cost, delivery effort, inference cost and the human attention consumed.

Use AI summaries to find themes worth checking against the original feedback. A summary does not establish cause, and an evaluation score covers only the cases and criteria used. Read how to evaluate AI behaviour and check model-based judgements.

Link each result to its research notes, dataset or test run. Keep participant information in the appropriate controlled location and summarise only what the decision needs. When evidence conflicts, record the conflict rather than averaging it into a reassuring conclusion.

Product, Design and Engineering should review feedback from use together. If evidence challenges the user need or intended behaviour, reopen Project Discovery; if it reveals a bounded implementation defect, route it to delivery. Change the product intent through a recorded decision; feedback does not automatically authorise model retraining or broader agent permissions.

Connect the measures chosen in Frame

Features shipped, prototypes generated, prompts submitted and lines of AI-generated code measure activity. They do not show user impact or business value. Define measures at each of these layers:

Suggested measurement layers; set local measures and thresholds before testing
LayerWhat it answers
User outcomeDid the user achieve the outcome that makes the product worthwhile?
Business outcomeDid the product create the intended value for the organisation?
Product behaviourDid users adopt the behaviour that should drive the outcome?
Leading indicatorsAre early signals moving in the expected direction?
Learning speed and costHow quickly and affordably did a hypothesis become credible evidence and a decision?
GuardrailsDid quality, safety, reliability, cost, privacy and fairness stay within tolerance?

Choose a value measure to steer by

Connect the resources spent, behaviours expected to help, useful user result and wider organisational benefit. This adapts the Defence Product Playbook’s ladder using the same terms as the success measures in step 2. Keep guardrails alongside those measures; see the source-adaptation note.

The metric ladder, adapted from the Defence Product Playbook
RungWhat it shows
1. Resources investedResources invested, such as team effort, funding or compute
2. Supporting measureA behaviour or capability expected to help produce the useful result; check that relationship
3. User-value measureThe intended outcome of solving the problem; the measure the team steers by
4. Organisational outcomeThe effect the organisation ultimately seeks; often slower to change than measures used to guide weekly work

The rows describe different questions, not stronger and weaker evidence. Confidence depends on the quality of the observations and the tested links between measures. The playbook recommends one value measure per problem that can move at least twice a year. This describes how often meaningful change can be observed. Explain how improving the measure contributes to the outcome above it, and test that relationship. Choose a review cadence suited to the product and decision, and carry it into the measurement plan.

Availability can serve different purposes in different products. For the asset-management example, treat uptime as a reliability guardrail: the application can be available while its records remain inaccurate. Usage is a useful supporting measure only when evidence links it to the intended benefit.

Ask whether the measure could improve while the intended outcome stays unchanged. Check the link between them. Keep useful operational measures and, unlike the playbook, consider self-reported outcomes such as satisfaction, effort and trust. Compare these with observed behaviour and service data, noting sampling and response biases. Check that measures are specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound (SMART).

The playbook’s value-cost ratio measures outcome delivered per annual cost and tracks change year on year. State the outcome units, costs included and measurement period. Compare ratios only when those units and cost boundaries are comparable, or a justified common valuation makes comparison possible. Financial return on investment (ROI) also needs justified monetary benefits and costs.

When measured value plateaus, investigate whether the product is sustaining an essential outcome or meeting an obligation before shifting investment. Maintenance may preserve mission value, supportability and risk controls even when the headline measure no longer rises.

Measures worth considering include:

  • Time to validated learning: elapsed time from an explicit hypothesis to credible evidence and a decision.
  • Cost per experiment: the cost of producing credible learning, including compute and human review.
  • Human attention ratio: the share of team time spent on users, strategy, judgement, difficult exceptions and learning, rather than producing documents and coordinating.
  • Product guardrails: task success, correction and escalation rates, model errors, latency, reliability, cost, privacy and safety incidents, fairness where material, and user trust.

Continue to Product implementation: readiness checks.

    Metric-ladder adaptation: this guide uses “resources invested” for effort, funding and compute, and “supporting measures” for behaviours or capabilities expected to influence value.
